Guardian live blog (Andrew Sparrow) | PUBLISHED: first 08.40 BST, updated 17.45 BST 21 Oct 2026 (paginated pages merged; [time] = block publish time BST)

[17.45 BST] Afternoon summary
The UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, a widely expected move that will nonetheless dismay environmental campaigners and a number of Labour MPs.
Miatta Fahnbulleh is leaning towards rejecting the giant Rosebank oilfield, the Guardian understands, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.
A cabinet split over Shabana Mahmood’s immigration policy has deepened after the energy secretary refused to say she backed plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK.
Reform UK has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time.
Reform UK says it has reported ITV to the police over its undercover racism exposé about the party, which it claims left some members “pyschologically damaged”. (See 3.50pm.)
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.

[16.53 BST] NEU says robust action on antisemitism in schools needed, but rejects reports call for teacher impartiality rules to be tightened
Richard Adams is the Guardian’s education editor.
The review of antisemitism in England’s schools and colleges by Sir David Bell has now been published, with the Department for Education saying it will adopt its recommendations including antisemitism training for education leaders, strengthened safeguarding guidance and improved reporting and investigation of antisemitic incidents.
 
 
 Bell’s full report goes into detail about the challenges that Jewish students and institutions face directly from antisemitism, as well as ways to tackle antisemitism in schools across the country.
 
 
 The review also talks about the external pressures that schools face from parents and other community members, noting:
Schools and colleges should make decisions based on safeguarding, professional conduct, employment law and evidence, not on who can generate the strongest public pressure campaign or out of fear of stoking community tensions.
Presenting the review to parliament, education secretary Lucy Powell said:
We have a duty to teach this generation and the next what antisemitism is, why it’s wrong and what happens when it takes hold. That goes for every school and college, whether or not they have Jewish staff and students.
Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union, said:
Robust action to challenge antisemitism is certainly needed because young people are exposed to antisemitic ideas and tropes, including on social media, and to influencers and figures who espouse violence. Educational experiences that empower young people to develop positive attitudes and respect for each other are critical.
But Kebede rejected the need for schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism or new rules on political impartiality, saying they would make it harder for schools to discuss complex world events. He said:
This report will not tackle antisemitism. It wrongly calls into question the professionalism of teachers. The existing rules on impartiality in the classroom are very clear and teachers take that responsibility very seriously.
 For three years, teachers have been responding to concerned pupils’ questions about this conflict. These classroom discussions are familiar territory, not uncharted ground.
The recommendations in the report include one saying the DfE “should strengthen guidance for schools on political impartiality” and another saying school leaders should “consider the appropriateness of political expression and identifiers in their respective settings”.

[16.35 BST] Karl Turner MP has Labour whip restored after apologising for 'overly robust' and 'unaceptable' conduct towards colleagues
Karl Turner has had the Labour whip restored after apologising for what he describes as an “overly robust” and “unacceptable” approach towards colleagues. He has admitted that his behaviour caused offence.
He has issued this statement and says he will not be making any further comment.
Turner had the whip suspended in March.

[16.25 BST] Burnham backs mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after parent-carer Matilda Davis’s death
Andy Burnham has backed mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after the “devastating” death of Matilda Davis, a parent-carer who killed herself minutes after meeting professionals, Josh Halliday reports.

[15.50 BST] Reform UK claims undercover racism exposé has left some of its members 'psychologically damaged' as it reports ITV to police
Reform UK says it has reported “multiple” ITV journalists, and the company’s board of directors, to the police on the grounds that their undercover reporters working on the exposé of racism in the party broke the law. The party says it will also be suing them for damages.
Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, posted this on social media summarising his party’s allegations.
Reform UK has reported ITV, its board, and its undercover reporters to the police.
 Some of the crimes carry up to 10 years in prison.
 They forged a passport.
 They directly interfered in elections and almost certainly altered the results. Being paid to “canvass” for Reform in crucial wards we lost by a few dozen votes.
 They lied to a veteran about their service and left him “violated”.
 This is unprecedented.
 The police are now involved.
 Scrutiny of political parties is one thing.
 But anyone breaking the law to try and ruin the lives of Reform’s staff, members or volunteers will be reported to the police and pursued relentlessly in the courts.
In a video setting out his case against ITV at greater length, Yusuf claimed ITV “psychologically damaged innocent and decent Reform staff and members who were not featured in any documentary”.
As an example of this, Yusuf said that one of the undercover reporters met a Reform UK member in Portsmouth who had served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He said:
One of the undercover reporters told him that they shared the same military background. That was a lie. The marine, believing him, took him for a drink. They spent hours talking about their service, and the marine shared deeply personal stories from the front line because he believed he was talking to a friend and a fellow soldier. He has told us he feels violated.
Yusuf also explained why he was alleging electoral interference. In Portsmouth two undercover reporters were tasked with delivering leaflets in one ward where Reform UK lost in the local elections by 24 votes, and in another ward where Reform UK lost by just 85 votes. Yusuf said these margins were smaller than the number of leaflets the undercover reporters were supposed to deliver.
But he did not assert in the video that they failed to deliver the leaflets, and he offered no evidence that they had done anything to suppress the Reform UK vote at the time.
Asked about the legal threats, an ITV spokesperson said:
ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest. All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch we would fully cooperate.
People tend to assume that a public interest defence will protect journalists from allegations of minor law-breaking if they are investigating wrongdoing. In fact, the law is more complicated than that, a public interest defence applies in some instances and not in others, and there are probably enough allegations in the Yusuf video to keep a media lawyer busy for days assessing the evidence.
But, in practice, it is rare for the criminal law to be used successfully against legitimate journalists. When the Crown Prosecution Service prosecuted police officers who had taken bribes, and the journalists who had paid them, under Operation Elveden, the officers were largely convicted but the journalists were largely acquitted. Juries seemed to accept they were operating in the public interest.
In the ITV case, the public interest case for the programme is particularly strong. Reform UK has accepted that some of the people exposed making racist comments should not be in the party – although it has also claimed they were not representative of the membership as a whole.

[14.45 BST] No 10 plays down Fahnbulleh's lack of support for home secretary's original ILR proposals
At the No 10 post-PMQs lobby briefing, Downing Street rejected suggestions that Miatta Fahnbulleh was undermining Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, with her comments about indefinite leave to remain (ILR) this morning. (See 10.44am and 11.34am.) A spokesperson said that Mahmood was consulting on the plans announced last year and that she is engaged in “a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place”. Asked about the Fahnbulleh interview, the spokesperson said:
The energy secretary made clear she backs reforms and the work that Shabana is doing. She was asked about specific elements of proposals that are subject to the results of the consultation.

[14.21 BST] Lindsay Hoyle accuses Fahnbulleh of 'immense discourtesy' to MPs after she misses Commons Jackdaw statement
In the Commons, Michael Shanks, the energy minister, is making a statement about the Jackdaw decision.
He is doing it because his boss, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is in Aberdeen.
Before he started, Lindsay Hoyle, the speaker, said it was an “immense discourtesy” to the Commons that Fahnbulleh was not there herself.
And he said it was “shameful” that her department announced the news to the media first.
He said:
It is simply not good enough that it was trailed by the press last night and announced all over the media this morning by the secretary of state before it could be properly scrutinised in this house.
 I’m sure there will be a leak inquiry, or is it that this department is deliberately briefing out to the media?
Hoyle said that, under the ministerial code, ministers were supposed to make important announcements to the Commons first.
Shanks told Hoyle that he respected what he had said, and that he would take these points back to the department.
Hoyle was not impressed. He said:
I’m sorry that Aberdeen is more important than the MPs they’ve elected.

[13.51 BST] Fahnbulleh leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
Miatta Fahnbulleh is leaning towards rejecting the giant Rosebank oilfield, the Guardian understands, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. Kiran Stacey has the story.

[13.49 BST] Donald Trump welcomes Jackdaw announcement
Judging by the latest post on Truth Social, it looks as thought the Jackdaw announcement may have made Fox News in the US this morning. This is from Donald Trump.

[13.38 BST] PMQs - snap verdict
That felt like quite a routine PMQs, but it was one that went quite well for Andy Burnham. It was not so much that he won; it was more that he emerged completely unscathed because none of Kemi Badenoch’s attack lines landed. It is always hard for an opposition leader to criticise a decision they agree with (Jackdaw), and so she tried the argument that Labour was to blame for rerunning the application process instead of fighting the legal challenge against the original decision all the way to the supreme court (where it may have lost anyway). Burnham’s response, that the Tories were to blame for mucking it up in the first place, was more convincing. After that Badenoch trotted through some very familiar lines on welfare and debt. It was hard to see what “story” she was trying to land, and it felt a bit as if she was not trying too hard. Maybe she is saving up her ammunition for her budget response next week.
Burnham also successfully seized the initiative with an announcement, about standing charges on gas bills. These are only worth about £100 a year, and presumably the money would be recouped from consumers in some other forms. Still, it’s news.
But what made Burnham’s performance quite strong today was not so much his standing charge teaser (which sounded like a hint for what might be in the budget) as his overall tone. One of the big complaints about PMQs is that MPs treat it as just a game. Badenoch herself is quite open about this, and she has said that she only started to do it well when she decided to view it like a panto. Burnham, though, can speak in the Commons with a degree of conviction and moral force that marks him out. We saw it today when he was talking about Aberfan, or social care, or Covid, or the importance of big decisions. This does not make him unique, and of course he is a professional politician, and he can equivocate as much as the rest of them. But at other moments he can convey seriousness and sincerity, rooted in lived experience, better than others. By comparison, Badenoch sounds glib.

[12.58 BST] Burnham says Reform UK has not done enough in response to ITV News racism exposé about 'politics of poison' in party
Zubir Ahmed (Lab) asked Burnham to condemn the revelations in the ITV News exposé of racism in Reform UK.
Burnham said all parties in the Commons should take a stand against racism. And he paid tribute in particular to migrant care workers.
He said MPs should “root out the politics of poison which has seeped far too far into our politics”.
And he said “the firmest of action” should be taken in reponse to these ITV revelations. But he said he was “still waiting to see the right level of action” from Reform UK.

[12.52 BST] Burnham backs call for mayor of Wessex, and says he wants full devolution for south-west of England
Edward Morello, the Lib Dem MP for West Dorset, asked Burnham if he would commit to having a mayor of Wessex by 2028.
Burnham said he would. He said he was “always happy to create more mayors”. He said he would like to see full devolution for the south-west of England. He says Cornish MPs were in No 10 North this week to speak about devolution deal.

[12.38 BST] Burnham says government will consider 'further measures' Royal Mail does not improve its 'unacceptable' service
Imogen Walker (Lab) said her constituents were suffering serious problems because Royal Mail delivery services were so bad.
Burnham replied:
Royal Mail’s service has been unacceptable for far too long. They have been asked in to see ministers on a regular basis. Ofcom is looking at the situation as well.
 Let’s be clear, they need to bring forward a plan to restore service standards to the level they need to be up. They need to do it quickly, or we will consider further measures.

[12.32 BST] Burnham ducks Lib Dem question about whether Elon Musk should have satellite licences restricted after 'beyond the pale' help for Putin
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, asked Burnham if he was going to wait until after the election until considering the case for joining the EU single market.
Burnham said at the UK-EU summit next month he would try to get a better deal covering food, energy and immigration. He went on:
If this house was to come together, it would give me the strongest position to go to that summit and get a good deal for.
Davey said, in the light of the PM’s position on Europe, “I feel that next week’s budget will not be the growth budget our country needs.”
He went on:
This week Ukraine’s defence system was seriously undermined by the US restricting access to Elon Musk’s Starlink system.
 Musk says that the order came from the White House, but the Telegraph and The Wall Street Journal have revealed that Musk put the idea to Donald Trump himself.
 Now, I understand the prime minister’s reluctance to criticise the present United States, but does he agree that directly aiding Putin in this way is beyond the pale? And will he work with European allies to prevent Elon Musk getting the licenses he wants? It would make our continent even more dependent on his satellite system.
Burnham said he had “concerns about any move that diminishes the military capability of Ukraine”. But he said the situation had to be handled carefully. The UK was working to help Ukraine, he said.
UPDATE: Burnham said:
Of course, I have concerns about any move that diminishes the military capability of Ukraine in the position in which it finds itself at this moment in time.
 Of course, he is right about that, and I am sure that sentiment is echoed right around this country. But it is a situation that is currently fragile and needs careful handling.”
 At this moment in time, I think we need to handle the situation carefully, so that we can bring back all sides to get the support behind President Zelensky and Ukraine.
 And I can assure him, the UK Government is working on every single level to bring that about.

[12.25 BST] Burnham defends Palestine Action ban, saying decision taken after 'rigorous and evidence-based process'
Claire Hanna (SDLP) asks about Sally Rooney’s books not being on sale in the UK, and invites Burnham to review the Palestine Action ban.
Burnham says:
When it comes to the prescription of Palestine Action, it followed a rigorous and evidence-based process that came before this house, endorsed by Parliament. The matter is alive, a legal case, so I won’t comment further than that.

[12.18 BST] Burnham defends taking action on 'small things', like train noise, but says he's taking 'big decisions' too
Badenoch says she has read the IMF report and it has downgrades the UK’s growth forecast.
We are spending more on interest payments than we do on schools, the army and the police combined. Meanwhile, the prime minister is worrying about loud music on trains. This is not serious.
She asks Burnham if he will cut welfare spending.
Burnham says he cut spending on his first day in office, on digital ID.
He goes on:
She asks about the big decisions. I want to come directly back to what she’s saying. I’m not going to apologise for doing the small things that help people have better lives. I’m not going to apologise for that.
 But I also take the big decisions that they have avoided for many years and let me go directly to one, directly to one social care.
 I grasped the nettle in a way that nobody on their side ever has, and I made a difficult spending decision to lay a path towards a National Care Service.
 Have they had the time to read the Covid inquiry report yesterday about the appalling state of social care as it went in to the pandemic? The hundreds of thousands of British people who suffered as a result of that, the lives that were lost.
 I need no lectures from the other side about taking tough decisions on social care.

[12.08 BST] Burnham says government considering removing standing charges from gas bills
Kemi Badenoch thanks Burnham for finally backing Jackdaw. The Tories approved it in 2022, she says. And rather than right the leftie activists who tried to block it in court. Labour appointed one of them as energy secretary, she says.
She asks Burnham to lift the ban on new licence applications.
Burnham says he has made a decision on something the Tories “messed up”.
He says the government has made a bridge to the future, the transition to clean energy.
He says he has asked the chancellor and the energy secretary to consider if standing charges can be removed from gas bills. They will report back “at the earliest opportunity”.

[11.42 BST] Total UK government debt hits £3tn for first time while inflation jumps to highest in nearly a year
In the light of her speech yesterday, it would be surprising if Kemi Badenoch does not ask about government spending. As Heather Stewart reports, the Treasury ran a higher than expected budget deficit of £24.5bn last month – and total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time.
Julia Kollewe has more on the business live blog.

[11.39 BST] Burnham faces Badenoch at PMQs
PMQs is starting soon.
Here is the list of MPs who have a question.

[11.36 BST] Government to crack down on ‘cosmetic cowboys’
The government has launched a crackdown on “cosmetic cowboys” performing liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs) on the high street in a bid to drive out rogue operators and raise standards across the board, the Press Association reports. PA says:
Ministers said that patients who choose to have cosmetic procedures deserve to know they are in safe hands and not risking their lives.
 The government also remains committed to bringing in a licensing scheme to ensure “lower risk” treatments such as Botox and lip fillers remain safe.
 Under the new rules, treatments that involve injecting fillers anywhere other than the face, such as BBLs, would be legally defined as cosmetic surgical procedures – meaning they can only be performing by qualified medics.
 Other high-risk treatments such as deep chemical peels and vampire facials – which use microneedling to inject platelets drawn from a patient’s own blood back into the face – would be restricted to doctors, dentists, some nurses, midwives and pharmacists.
 Those who flout the rules could be hit with unlimited fines or fixed penalties up to £4,000.

[10.44 BST] Fahnbulleh declines to back Mahmood's proposal to make some migrant workers wait 15 years for indefinite leave to remain
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has declined to back the home secretary’s plan to make some migrant workers wait up to 15 years before they can apply for permanent residency in the UK (indefinite leave to remain, or ILF).
Earlier this week, it emerged that she published a comment criticising the plan on her constituency website – before she removed it supposedly because it was a poorly-phrased summary of her position drafted by an aide.
In interviews today, asked specifically if she backed migrants having to wait for up to 15 years for ILR, she refused to support this proposal.
Asked about this on Sky News, she said:
We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution.
 And so there is a package of reforms. The home secretary [Shabana Mahmood] has been consulting on this. She’s looking at the range of responses, and she will come out with the measures that we take forward.
 No-one can look at our immigration system – and I say this as someone that came to this country as a refugee – and not believe that it’s broken and not believe that we need to fundamentally reform it.
 But our principles has to be a system where we’ve got control, but ultimately a system that when people do come to this country, they are able to integrate, they are able to contribute, and that we both respect but also value that contribution.
Mahmood is proposing most migrant workers should have to wait 10 years for ILF, not five years as now. But under her plans foreign care workers would have to wait 15 years.
Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child refugee from Liberia.
In its splash story today, the Times says Mahmood is “fighting a rearguard action to save her migration reforms in the face of mounting public criticism from cabinet colleagues”.
The report says:
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, is considering exempting care workers from plans to extend the qualifying period for claiming indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five years to 15 years.
 However, the Home Office has argued that the move could backfire because it could lead to an exodus of foreign care workers from their jobs once they gained permanent residence and were no longer bound by the terms of their visas.

[10.02 BST] Climate campaigners condemn ‘maddening’ decision to approve Jackdaw gasfield
Fiona Harvey, the Guardian’s environment editor, has more here on climate campaigners condemning the Jackdaw decision.

[10.00 BST] Jackdaw development will create 27 new jobs, and safeguard 273 existing ones, government says
The government itself has admitted that the Jackdaw development will only create a small number of new jobs. This is from the small print of its news release.
The developer estimates that Jackdaw will create 27 new direct jobs and safeguard 273 existing jobs that would otherwise be lost. The developer also estimates that the project will add around £2.9 billion to the UK economy.
 Over its lifetime, Jackdaw is estimated to produce gas with an energy equivalent to around 40 million barrels of oil.

[09.37 BST] Healey announces initial £2bn funding for Energy Wealth Fund, which will allocate some North Sea tax revenue for renewables
Alongside the Jackdaw announcement, the government has said it is setting up an Energy Wealth Fund. This will in effect ringfence some North Sea oil and gas tax revenues for investment in renewables.
In its news release, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero says:
The chancellor is also announcing today the establishment of a new Energy Wealth Fund, which will use tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects and support the green transition. Reflecting our commitment to the North Sea, this will start with an initial £2bn injection of funding, with future revenues from the North Sea flowing into the fund over time …
 The Energy Wealth Fund will support investment in the renewable and low carbon energy industries that will power Britain’s future. It will help ensure more value from Britain’s energy resources is invested for the long term, supporting the green transition and creating a lasting national asset for future generations.
John Healey, the chancellor, said:
Through our new Energy Wealth Fund, we will invest in the clean energy industries of the future, creating jobs, driving growth and strengthening Britain’s energy security.

[09.26 BST] Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says approving Jackdaw gasfield won't lead to cheaper energy bills
In her interviews this morning, Miatta Fahnbulleh confirmed that approving the Jackdaw gasfield would not lead to cheaper energy bills for consumers.
On LBC Nick Ferrari asked if the decision meant that his listeners would have lower bills. Fahnbulleh replied:
No, and I think it’s really important that we’re honest about this. That was not a consideration in the decision because it won’t mean cheaper bills.
 This was about energy security and having homegrown energy, and it was also because we thought it was compatible with our with our climate commitments.
Fahnbulleh did accept that the price of energy was a “fundamental” issue. But she said the government was addressing this in other ways, like removing VAT from electricity bills.

[09.14 BST] UK inflation rises by more than expected to 3.5% as war drives up fuel prices
UK inflation climbed by more than expected in September to 3.5% after a surge in prices from the conflict in the Middle East that has pushed up the cost of diesel to record levels, Phillip Inman reports.

[08.40 BST] Labour accused of ‘climate vandalism’ by Green leader Polanski after Jackdaw gasfield approved
Good morning. After months of delay, the government has taken a decision on one of the most difficult climate crisis/energy supply challenges on the table. It has approved the Jackdaw gasfield, east of Aberdeen. Peter Walker and Kiran Stacey have the story here.
Here is the government’s news release. And if you want to all the technical documents relating to the decision, you will find them here.
At the last election, Labour said it would not approve new oil and gas licences for the North Sea, but that it would allow existing projects to go ahead. But two projects that had been approved by the Tories – Jackdaw, and the Rosebank oilfield – were blocked by the courts who ordered a rethink, and Labour decided to treat them as existing projects, not brand new ones. But that did not mean Jackdaw and Rosebank were automatically going to be approved.
Over the past 12 months or so, largely as a result of high global energy prices, the public and political debate has shifted, and pressure to allow more ongoing North Sea extraction got stronger. Today’s decision did not come as a surprise. But the Rosebank decision will be a much tougher one because its carbon emissions are far higher than Jackdaw’s, and the environmental argument against it is stronger.
In a statement, Andy Burnham described today’s decision as an example of the “pragmatic approach” he wants to take to energy policy. He said:
I welcome the energy secretary’s decision, which will protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter. At a time when people are really struggling, it’s right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help.
 We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea. We’re also establishing a new Energy Wealth Fund to invest in renewable energy, support the green transition and help reduce energy bills over the long-term.
Some Labour figures are alarmed at the decision, but so far there has been very little public criticism of the move from the party’s MPs. The other main parties support Jackdaw going ahead. But the Greens have denounced the decision very strongly. This is from their leader, Zack Polanski.
This is climate vandalism.
 Today’s decision by Labour is a betrayal of all of our futures, Labour has abandoned all credibility in the fight against climate change.
 The energy secretary has herself said it will make no difference to energy bills; the health secretary has admitted the summer heatwave added to pressure on the NHS, and the industry’s own assessment is that it will create only 27 jobs.
 This is a victory for Shell over the people.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning: Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, is on a visit to a gas terminal in Peterhead to promote the Jackdaw decision.
Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.
After 12.30pm: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, is expected to make a statement to MPs about the Jackdaw decision.
2.10pm: Michelle O’Neill, Northern Ireland’s first minister, and Emma Little-Pengelly, the deputy first minister, give evidence to Stormont’s executive office committee.
Afternoon: Burnham welcomes Haitham bin Tariq, the Sultan of Oman, to Downing Street.

Zia Yusuf claims undercover investigation broke the law as broadcaster stands by its journalism

Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, posted this on social media summarising his party’s allegations.

double quotation markReform UK has reported ITV, its board, and its undercover reporters to the police.

Some of the crimes carry up to 10 years in prison.

They directly interfered in elections and almost certainly altered the results. Being paid to “canvass” for Reform in crucial wards we lost by a few dozen votes.

They lied to a veteran about their service and left him “violated”.

Scrutiny of political parties is one thing.

But anyone breaking the law to try and ruin the lives of Reform’s staff, members or volunteers will be reported to the police and pursued relentlessly in the courts.

In a video setting out his case against ITV at greater length, Yusuf claimed ITV “psychologically damaged innocent and decent Reform staff and members who were not featured in any documentary”.

As an example of this, Yusuf said that one of the undercover reporters met a Reform UK member in Portsmouth who had served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He said:

double quotation markOne of the undercover reporters told him that they shared the same military background. That was a lie. The marine, believing him, took him for a drink. They spent hours talking about their service, and the marine shared deeply personal stories from the front line because he believed he was talking to a friend and a fellow soldier. He has told us he feels violated.

Yusuf also explained why he was alleging electoral interference. In Portsmouth two undercover reporters were tasked with delivering leaflets in one ward where Reform UK lost in the local elections by 24 votes, and in another ward where Reform UK lost by just 85 votes. Yusuf said these margins were smaller than the number of leaflets the undercover reporters were supposed to deliver.

But he did not assert in the video that they failed to deliver the leaflets, and he offered no evidence that they had done anything to suppress the Reform UK vote at the time.

Asked about the legal threats, an ITV spokesperson said:

double quotation markITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest. All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch we would fully cooperate.

People tend to assume that a public interest defence will protect journalists from allegations of minor law-breaking if they are investigating wrongdoing. In fact, the law is more complicated than that, a public interest defence applies in some instances and not in others, and there are probably enough allegations in the Yusuf video to keep a media lawyer busy for days assessing the evidence.

But, in practice, it is rare for the criminal law to be used successfully against legitimate journalists. When the Crown Prosecution Service prosecuted police officers who had taken bribes, and the journalists who had paid them, under Operation Elveden, the officers were largely convicted but the journalists were largely acquitted. Juries seemed to accept they were operating in the public interest.

In the ITV case, the public interest case for the programme is particularly strong. Reform UK has accepted that some of the people exposed making racist comments should not be in the party – although it has also claimed they were not representative of the membership as a whole.

Miatta Fahnbulleh is leaning towards rejecting the giant Rosebank oilfield, the Guardian understands, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.

A cabinet split over Shabana Mahmood’s immigration policy has deepened after the energy secretary refused to say she backed plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK.

Reform UK has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time.

They were protesting about the Jackdaw decision announced today, and also urging the government not to approve the Rosebank oil field, where the decision is pending.

Robin Wells, director of the campaign group, said:

double quotation markThis decision is salted with the tears of every Nepalese person who saw someone they loved swept away in a river tsunami and it’s stained with the blood of everyone in Valencia who died as cars afloat in mud, sewage and enough rainwater for a year collided into their bodies in streets that had become rivers.

Although we cannot right now hear people in Australia, LA and Portugal crying in fear as their homes and worlds burn, these are the knock-on consequences of corporations that continue to drill fossil fuels and the governments that permit it, knowing the damage caused.

Our government must not double down on madness now. They must not lap-up industry propaganda again for the next North Sea project in their in-tray. If they believe in a future that protects people’s homes and safety, not endangers them, they must stop Rosebank.

Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockShare38m ago17.23 BSTThe Department for Education has announced that Simon Ridley will be its new permanent secretary. Ridley will move from the Home Office, where he has been second permanent secretary.

He will replace Susan Acland-Hood, who is taking a new job outside government. Acland-Hood became head of the DfE in 2020 after the previous permanent secretary, Jonathan Slater, was sacked during Covid after the department oversaw a botched exam grading system that infuriated parents and pupils.

1h ago16.53 BSTNEU says robust action on antisemitism in schools needed, but rejects reports call for teacher impartiality rules to be tightenedRichard AdamsRichard Adams is the Guardian’s education editor.

The review of antisemitism in England’s schools and colleges by Sir David Bell has now been published, with the Department for Education saying it will adopt its recommendations including antisemitism training for education leaders, strengthened safeguarding guidance and improved reporting and investigation of antisemitic incidents.
 
 
 Bell’s full report goes into detail about the challenges that Jewish students and institutions face directly from antisemitism, as well as ways to tackle antisemitism in schools across the country.
 
 
 The review also talks about the external pressures that schools face from parents and other community members, noting:

double quotation markSchools and colleges should make decisions based on safeguarding, professional conduct, employment law and evidence, not on who can generate the strongest public pressure campaign or out of fear of stoking community tensions.

Presenting the review to parliament, education secretary Lucy Powell said:

double quotation markWe have a duty to teach this generation and the next what antisemitism is, why it’s wrong and what happens when it takes hold. That goes for every school and college, whether or not they have Jewish staff and students.

Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union, said:

double quotation markRobust action to challenge antisemitism is certainly needed because young people are exposed to antisemitic ideas and tropes, including on social media, and to influencers and figures who espouse violence. Educational experiences that empower young people to develop positive attitudes and respect for each other are critical.

But Kebede rejected the need for schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism or new rules on political impartiality, saying they would make it harder for schools to discuss complex world events. He said:

double quotation markThis report will not tackle antisemitism. It wrongly calls into question the professionalism of teachers. The existing rules on impartiality in the classroom are very clear and teachers take that responsibility very seriously.

For three years, teachers have been responding to concerned pupils’ questions about this conflict. These classroom discussions are familiar territory, not uncharted ground.

The recommendations in the report include one saying the DfE “should strengthen guidance for schools on political impartiality” and another saying school leaders should “consider the appropriateness of political expression and identifiers in their respective settings”.

double quotation markIt is simply not good enough that it was trailed by the press last night and announced all over the media this morning by the secretary of state before it could be properly scrutinised in this house.

I’m sure there will be a leak inquiry, or is it that this department is deliberately briefing out to the media?

Hoyle said that, under the ministerial code, ministers were supposed to make important announcements to the Commons first.

double quotation markI’m sorry that Aberdeen is more important than the MPs they’ve elected.

View image in fullscreenPost by Donald Trump Photograph: Truth SocialShare4h ago13.38 BSTPMQs - snap verdictThat felt like quite a routine PMQs, but it was one that went quite well for Andy Burnham. It was not so much that he won; it was more that he emerged completely unscathed because none of Kemi Badenoch’s attack lines landed. It is always hard for an opposition leader to criticise a decision they agree with (Jackdaw), and so she tried the argument that Labour was to blame for rerunning the application process instead of fighting the legal challenge against the original decision all the way to the supreme court (where it may have lost anyway). Burnham’s response, that the Tories were to blame for mucking it up in the first place, was more convincing. After that Badenoch trotted through some very familiar lines on welfare and debt. It was hard to see what “story” she was trying to land, and it felt a bit as if she was not trying too hard. Maybe she is saving up her ammunition for her budget response next week.

Burnham also successfully seized the initiative with an announcement, about standing charges on gas bills. These are only worth about £100 a year, and presumably the money would be recouped from consumers in some other forms. Still, it’s news.

But what made Burnham’s performance quite strong today was not so much his standing charge teaser (which sounded like a hint for what might be in the budget) as his overall tone. One of the big complaints about PMQs is that MPs treat it as just a game. Badenoch herself is quite open about this, and she has said that she only started to do it well when she decided to view it like a panto. Burnham, though, can speak in the Commons with a degree of conviction and moral force that marks him out. We saw it today when he was talking about Aberfan, or social care, or Covid, or the importance of big decisions. This does not make him unique, and of course he is a professional politician, and he can equivocate as much as the rest of them. But at other moments he can convey seriousness and sincerity, rooted in lived experience, better than others. By comparison, Badenoch sounds glib.

5h ago13.01 BSTDavid Davis (Con) asks if the PM would speak to the defence secretary to stop British agencies acting with “credulous complicity with our enemies trying to use lawfare against our soldiers”.

He was referring in particular to a Sunday Times report at the weekend about how SAS soldiers were hounded over “bogus allegations”.

Burnham said he would be happy to meet Davis to discuss this. He wanted to give an assurance to solidiers that the government would “always have their back” and treat them fairly.

double quotation markThe Sunday Times reported on its front page how Ministry of Defence police attempted to prosecute five members of the SAS over bogus allegations made by our enemies. They arrested the soldiers and subjected them to continuous—and frankly incompetent—investigation for three years while they were fighting ISIS on our behalf. That action has travelled like a shockwave through Hereford, destroying morale and undermining one of our best fighting units. Nobody wants to put soldiers above the law, but will the Prime Minister speak to the Defence Secretary and stop British agencies acting with credulous complicity with enemies that are trying to use lawfare against our soldiers?

double quotation markI am aware of the high levels of concern among those who served in the SAS, and [Davis] has spoken to that. Without going into all the details, I am happy to meet him to discuss the case and see how we can resolve some of the issues that arise from it, giving an assurance to people who served this country that we will have their back and always treat them fairly.
